# Neros Secures $75M Series B Funding, Joins Army Program with Sequoia Lead

Neros, based in El Segundo, California, has successfully secured $75 million in Series B funding, led by Sequoia Capital, with additional investments from Vy Capital US and Interlagos\. This new influx of capital follows a period of rapid growth for the company, highlighted by significant revenue increases and key customer acquisitions\.

- Advertisement -

## Strategic Partnerships and Military Contracts

The funding round occurs shortly after Neros completed substantial customer deployments, including a large purchase order from the U\.S\. Marine Corps\. Furthermore, the company has been selected as a primary supplier of First-Person View \(FPV\) drones for the U\.S\. Army under the Purpose-Built Attritable Systems \(PBAS\) program\.

### Funding Utilization and Production Expansion

The latest investment raises Neros’ total capital to over $120 million\. It will facilitate expanding the company’s industrial capacity, particularly focusing on the mass production of its Archer and Archer Strike drone platforms, as well as Ground Control Systems\.

- Strengthening a domestic, China-free supply chain
- Investing in allied component suppliers
- Enhancing research and development for next-generation autonomous systems

This funding will support Neros’ vertically integrated manufacturing strategy, allowing it to control essential production stages\. The outcome is expected to enhance the delivery of advanced FPV capabilities to American military forces\.

## Leadership and Future Directions

Soren Monroe-Anderson, CEO of Neros, emphasized the significance of this fundraising as a culmination of over two years of growth and product development\. He acknowledged the dedication of the Neros team and their investors’ faith in reshoring America’s drone manufacturing capabilities\.

- Advertisement -

According to Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, this successful funding round underscores the urgent need for reliable drone systems, with Neros emerging as a crucial player in the defense industry\. Achal Upadhyaya, Founder and CEO of Interlagos, highlighted the potential for Neros to become a leading factory for drone production in the United States\.

### Global Expansion and Commitment

Neros is not only focusing on U\.S\. military contracts but is also expanding its presence internationally\. The company plans to enhance operations in Ukraine and is already supplying drones to the UK Ministry of Defense\.

The strategic global outreach allows Neros to meet the urgent demands of international customers while stabilizing its production requirements\. To support this expansion, Neros is actively hiring across its locations, including Los Angeles, Kyiv, London, and Washington D\.C\.

With a commitment to address the production challenges faced by Western allies, Neros aims to lead the development of a resilient drone manufacturing base\. The company continues to explore innovative solutions for advancing drone technology while securing an advantageous position against adversaries\.

# Neros Technologies raises $250M to deploy its defense drones by the end of 2026 - The Robot Report

Neros Archer is a FPV drone built for modular payloads and resilient communications\. \| Source: Neros

Neros Inc\. this week announced it raised $250 million in a Series C round\. This brought the drone defense contractor to a $2\.5 billion valuation\.

“This newest round of funding accelerates Neros into a multi-capability drone manufacturer,” stated Soren Monroe-Anderson, co-founder and CEO of Neros\. “Our mission to produce 1 million drones per year hasn’t changed, but the span of drones and mission sets we can support are multiplying\. Our core business has seen explosive growth since our last financing round in November, and this added capital gets our systems into war-fighter hands faster, and at the scale needed for decisive outcomes on the battlefield\.”

Founded in 2023, Neros has major contracts with the U\.S\. Army and Marine Corps, as well as contracts with every component of U\.S\. Special Operations Command \(SOCOM\) and half a dozen allied countries\. The El Segundo, Calif\.-based company is partnering with allies across Europe via its U\.K\. subsidiary, as well as other allied nations across Asia and the Middle East in support of their own defense and sovereign manufacturing needs\.

## Neros plans for deployments by the end of 2026

Neros Technologies said it plans to use the funds to accelerate the development and production ramps for new drone programs including Archer AI and Bandit\. Archer AI is a first-person view \(FPV\) platform augmented with autonomy features including Terminal Guidance and GPS-denied Position Hold\.

Bandit is a c-UAS interceptor drone intended to counter Class 2 and 3 drone threats including Shahed-style systems\.

Neros is developing both platforms with the hardware and compute required for multi-asset control, often termed “swarming\.” The company plans to deploy Archer AI and Bandit in combat theaters by the end of 2026\.

## Investors support vertical stack

Sequoia Capital and American Strategic Technology Fund \(ASTF\) co-led the round\. Interlagos, Valor Equity Partners, Allen & Co\., Thiel Capital, Spark Capital, and Dylan Field also participated in the round\.

Neros previously raised $75 million in Series B funding in November 2025\.

Through owning the core technology, vertically integrating its component stack, and using its pre-existing domestic production capacity, Neros said it is positioned to deliver credible deterrence by building millions of aerial drones per year for America and its allies\.

By 2028, Neros claimed that it will produce 1 million drones per year across a range of capabilities including long range strike, close-quarters combat, and interceptors\.

## Funding for defense drones heats up

With ongoing wars in Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran, funding for defense drones has increased\. Earlier this week, Cambridge Aerospace raised $300 million in Series C funding, bringing its valuation to $3\.4 billion\. The defense drone developer said it plans to expand its manufacturing capabilities to deliver on existing and new contracts\.

Last month, Quantum Systems raised $1\.2 billion\. The company develops, designs, and produces fully autonomous drones for frontline forces\.

In June, Mach Industries, a manufacturer of uncrewed defense systems, raised $300 million\. In May, HavocAI, a provider of autonomous defense systems, raised $100 million\.

In additino, Ondas Inc\. last month acquired DZYNE Technologies LLC, an Irvine, Calif\.-based defense technology company, for $875\.8 million\.

# Neros Raises $250 Million Series C At $2\.5 Billion Valuation To Scale Autonomous And Interceptor Drone Programs

By Amit Chowdhry Yesterday at 10:44 AM

Neros Technologies has raised $250 million in Series C funding at a $2\.5 billion post-money valuation to accelerate development and production of its autonomous and interceptor drone programs\. The round was co-led by Sequoia Capital and American Strategic Technology Fund, with participation from Interlagos, Valor Equity Partners, Allen & Company, Thiel Capital, Spark Capital and Dylan Field\.

The new funding will support production ramps for several drone programs, including Archer AI and Bandit\.

Archer AI is an FPV drone platform augmented with autonomous capabilities including Terminal Guidance and GPS-denied Position Hold\.

Bandit is a counter-UAS interceptor designed to address Class 2 and Class 3 drone threats, including Shahed-style systems\.

Neros is also developing the hardware and compute infrastructure required for multi-asset control, often referred to as swarming, while aiming to preserve the low-cost characteristics needed for large-scale deployment\.

The company expects both Archer AI and Bandit to be deployed in combat theaters by the end of 2026\.

Neros said the expanded product portfolio is intended to give the company capabilities across the mass-produced small-drone market, spanning manually operated FPV systems enhanced with autonomous strike capabilities, counter-UAS interceptors and coordinated multi-drone operations\.

The company is pursuing a vertically integrated strategy that includes ownership of core technologies, component integration and domestic production capacity\.

Neros ultimately plans to manufacture millions of drones annually for the U\.S\. and allied countries, with a goal of reaching production of 1 million drones per year by 2028\.

Its planned product portfolio includes systems for long-range strike, close-quarters combat and drone interception\.

Neros currently has major contracts with the U\.S\. Army and Marine Corps, along with contracts across every component of U\.S\. Special Operations Command and approximately half a dozen allied countries\.

The company is also expanding internationally through its U\.K\. subsidiary and partnerships with allied countries across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, including efforts supporting sovereign defense manufacturing\.

**KEY QUOTE:**

*“This newest round of funding accelerates Neros into a multi-capability drone manufacturer\. Our mission to produce one million drones per year hasn’t changed, but the span of drones and mission sets we can support are multiplying\.”*

*“Our core business has seen explosive growth since our last financing round in November, and this added capital gets our systems into warfighter hands faster, and at the scale needed for decisive outcomes on the battlefield\.”*

**Soren Monroe-Anderson, Co-Founder and CEO of Neros Technologies**

Soren Monroe-Anderson, a champion drone racer, was only 20 years old when he first tried to sell his drones to the U\.S\. military\. He was building them for Ukrainian forces in his parents’ garage with a friend\.

The military was not interested\.

“‘You can’t just waltz into the Pentagon as 21-year-olds and sell weapon systems to the DOD,’” said the friend, Olaf Hichwa, recalling the response from a senior Department of Defense official\.

But two years later, Monroe-Anderson, now 22, and Hichwa, who just turned 24, are selling drones to the U\.S\. Army\.

Neros, the company they founded in 2023, has been selected to supply its signature drones, called Archer, to the Army, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times\. Neros is one of three American drone manufacturers picked as vendors for the first phase of an Army program that is buying low-cost, expendable drones\.

Although specific financial terms have not been disclosed, the Trump administration has budgeted more than $36 million for the “Purpose-Built Attritable Systems” program in 2026\.

Neros’ selection comes as military leaders are scrambling to catch up with adversaries who have the ability to mass produce small drones, which have become crucial to modern warfare\. The Army aims to buy at least 1 million drones in the next two to three years, Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll told Reuters\.

Although the government shutdown complicated the military’s efforts to buy drones, some contracts already in the pipeline are moving forward\.

The Army contract has been closely watched as a bellwether of which American drone companies will dominate the market\. For Neros, it comes on the heels of raising $75 million in venture funding, led by Sequoia Capital, and receiving a $17 million Marine Corps contract for thousands of drones, as well as an international drone coalition contract to supply 6,000 drones to Ukraine\.

Neros’ latest round of funding closed this month, bringing the total raised by the startup to $121 million and cementing Monroe-Anderson’s and Hichwa’s status as wunderkinds of the emerging U\.S\. drone industry\.

The Defense Innovation Unit, an experimental part of the Pentagon with headquarters in Silicon Valley, has been championing Neros for more than a year, with some drone specialists at the unit affectionately referring to Monroe-Anderson and Hichwa as “the boys\.”

At a flyoff in Alaska this past summer, military officials crowded around Monroe-Anderson as he piloted his drone unmolested toward a device that tried unsuccessfully to jam it\. A Neros Archer was one of several drones buzzing around Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July when he made a video announcement of policy changes aimed at turbocharging domestic production\.

In an interview in May, Maj\. Steven Atkinson of the Marine Corps Warfighting Lab recounted searching for American companies willing to supply small drones like the ones being used in Ukraine for less than $2,000 per unit\. He came up empty — until he found Neros\.

“They were pretty young, but they did FPVs,” recalled Atkinson, referring to first-person view drones, which are flown by pilots wearing special goggles to see video feeds from the drone’s camera while using a joystick controller to navigate around obstacles\.

“What they have been able to accomplish is unheard-of,” he said\.

Monroe-Anderson and Hichwa gained their expertise from the world of competitive drone racing\. Monroe-Anderson, who attended high school in New Hampshire, and Hichwa, who grew up in Maryland, spent their teen years building drones from kits and components they ordered from China\. They were so focused on flying and racing that they skipped much of school and their senior proms\. Neither has a college degree\.

The two met in 2017 at a drone-racing competition in Muncie, Indiana, and quickly began trading ideas about how to make their drones fly faster\.

Monroe-Anderson was the better racer, winning the MultiGP World Championship in 2020\. Hichwa was known for his engineering prowess\. “He’s a mad genius,” said David Spencer, a fellow racer\.

In an attempt to best Monroe-Anderson’s drone, Hichwa designed a circuit board for his own drone that was lighter than the ones on the market, soldering it himself\. He eventually bought an industrial machine from China that mass-produced them, selling them to other drone racers for $30 apiece during his junior year\. An upgraded version is used in Neros’ Archer\.

Despite their racing pedigree, challenges remain\. Drone racers tend to build systems that are fast and nimble, and require a certain level of mastery\. Neros typically trains soldiers on Archer drones for five days\. By contrast, DJI, the Chinese company that produces more than 75% of the world’s commercial drones, is known for drones that can be flown without any special training\.

And the skill it takes to make one racing drone is different from the expertise required to manufacture tens of thousands\. At Neros’ factory in El Segundo, California, about 20 technicians assemble roughly 2,000 drones per month by hand\.

It has been especially challenging to make cheap drones without Chinese parts\. Virtually everything they used as teenagers — propellers, motors, batteries, radios, cameras — came from Shenzhen, China\. But to sell to the U\.S\. military, Neros had to build a U\.S\. supply chain and prove that its drones do not contain critical components from China\.

Vendors in the United States “would laugh at us,” Hichwa said\. American-made radios could cost as much as $10,000 when he was shopping around for one that cost $30\. The founders quickly realized that they would have to build parts themselves and seek suppliers outside the defense industry\.

Instead of using computer chips common in military equipment that cost hundreds of dollars apiece, Neros used one designed for parking meters, which cost $1 each, Hichwa said\.

Their inspiration to build a drone company grew out of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which turned their high school hobby into a world-changing technology\. Ukrainians were beating back Russian forces with simple quadcopters jury-rigged with explosives\. In the summer of 2023, Hichwa was working at Skywalk, an artificial intelligence startup in Palo Alto, California, when Monroe-Anderson showed up at his job, begging him to make drones again\. Monroe-Anderson, who opted to forgo college for the time being, had become fixated with helping Ukraine\.

Hichwa took it on as a side project and quickly got sucked in\. They conferred on the phone with Ukrainians whom Monroe-Anderson had met on social media and made dozens of drones that snapped together in stacks that were easy to transport\. That fall, they went to Kyiv and distributed their drones to Ukrainian soldiers, collecting feedback about how they flew\. They met Deputy Prime Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who is also the country’s minister of digital transformation, who told them that anyone who wanted to supply drones to Ukraine had to be able to produce at least 5,000 per month\.

The trip underscored what they already knew: America is vulnerable\. Russia and China produced millions of drones a year, while the United States barely made 100,000\.

They set up shop in El Segundo, a hotbed for the aerospace industry, where their passion attracted the attention of venture capitalists and Peter Thiel, who eventually gave Monroe-Anderson a Thiel fellowship\.

“When we meet founders like that, we bet on their trajectory,” said Ian Rountree of Cantos, a venture capital firm that led their angel round\. He was impressed that Monroe-Anderson had managed to attract employees who were far more senior, including Sean Wood, the company’s chief operating officer, who had worked at SpaceX for 12 years\. Neros employs 80 people, and virtually all them are older than its founders\.

But mass production remains a challenge\. Last year, Hichwa traveled to Shenzen to meet the Chinese suppliers who had sent him drone parts when he was a teenage racer\. They showed him around their factories as a valued customer, never suspecting that he planned to open a plant of his own\. One factory that made the brand of hobbyist drones he flew in high school was now churning out 1,000 drones per day for the Russian military, he said\.

“They are, to a certain degree, my friends,” Hichwa said\. “But we found ourselves on opposite sides of an armed conflict\.”

He said he tried to remember as much as he could about the machinery they used, awed by what it would take for Neros to catch up\.

“We’re barely scraping 2,000 a month,” he said\. “And they’re doing that in two days\.”

# Neros Reportedly Raises $250 Million At $2\.5 Billion Valuation

By Amit Chowdhry Today at 10:44 AM

Neros Technologies has reached a $2\.5 billion valuation after raising $250 million in a new financing, according to Bloomberg\. This roughly triples the defense technology company’s value as demand grows for domestically manufactured military drones\. Sequoia Capital and American Strategic Technology Fund reportedly co-led the round, with participation from Thiel Capital and other existing investors\.

The new valuation represents a substantial increase from Neros’ November 2025 Series B, when private-market data placed the company’s post-money valuation at approximately $794 million\.

Neros has not yet publicly detailed the new financing, and the amount raised and participating investors were not available in the sources reviewed\.

The company previously raised $75 million in a Series B led by Sequoia Capital, with participation from Vy Capital US and Interlagos\. That round brought Neros’ total capital raised at the time to more than $120 million\.

Neros said the Series B capital was intended to expand industrial capacity, scale production of its Archer and Archer Strike drone platforms and Ground Control Systems, and strengthen a China-free supply chain through vertically integrated manufacturing and investments in allied component suppliers\.

The company has continued to scale rapidly since that financing\. Neros recently expanded into Millennium One, a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Torrance, California, as part of an initiative to increase its production capacity by approximately 100 times\.

Neros has also reported surpassing production of 1,000 drones in a single week at the Torrance facility\.

The manufacturing expansion comes alongside significant growth in government business\.

Neros recently secured a U\.S\. Army contract worth up to $500 million to supply its Archer first-person-view drones\. The contract is an indefinite-delivery arrangement, meaning the full $500 million is not guaranteed, but it represents one of the largest opportunities awarded to the young drone manufacturer\.

Neros was producing approximately 1,200 drones per week as of July and has set a goal of reaching annual production capacity of one million drones by 2028\.

Its flagship Archer platform is a low-cost FPV military drone designed for use in contested environments\. The company has also developed Archer Strike for kinetic applications and supporting ground-control technologies\.

Neros was founded in 2023 by former competitive drone racers Soren Monroe-Anderson and Olaf Hichwa\. The company initially focused on building drones that could compete economically with Chinese systems while relying on American and allied-country supply chains\.

Its fundraising history reflects that manufacturing strategy\. Before the Series B, Neros raised approximately $35 million in a Series A led by Vy Capital and $10\.9 million across earlier seed financing backed by investors including Sequoia Capital\.

The jump to a $2\.5 billion valuation comes as Neros transitions from a venture-backed drone developer into a larger-scale defense manufacturer with growing U\.S\. military programs and significant investments in domestic production capacity\.

By Charlie Leffler

On Friday afternoon, Louisville center Lori Nero sat on the floor of a Sports Information Department office anxiously watching television as names were called off in this year’s WNBA Draft\. Though she expected her name to eventually be called, she was still nervous\.

The first round of selections ended without Nero’s name being called but she was not upset because did not expect to be chosen in that round\. “I pretty much thought it should be somewhere around the second round,” said Nero, “not too much lower than that\.”

Only the first round of selections were televised locally so the group of watchers had to switch to viewing the remaining rounds on a laptop\. One by one the name were called out then with the 19th pick overall, the Houston Comets Announced they would be selecting Louisville’s Lori Nero\. “I can’t believe it still,” said Nero, “I’m very elated\.”

With the draft, Nero became only the second U of L women’s basketball player to be selected in the WNBA Draft and the highest ever for Louisville\. Nero was also the first Conference USA player selected in the draft which also meant a lot to her\. Despite the fact that the Cardinals did not perform well during the conference season, Nero’s performance was enough to gain her recognition\. “That says a lot about what I did this season in the conference and that I got recognized for it,” she said\.

Even though she has been chosen to play professionally, Nero believes it will be a while before the fact actually sinks in\. “Until I actually am surrounded by the environment and until I am actually on the team then I will believe it\.”

Nero, a native of Baton Rouge, La\., becomes the second Louisville player to be drafted\. Jill Morton was drafted in the third round with the 34th pick of the 2000 WNBA draft by the Charlotte Sting\.

Nero spent one season at the University of Louisville after transferring from Auburn University\. She made an impressive mark in just one season, leading the team in scoring and rebounding with 17\.4 points and 9\.4 rebounds per game\. Nero also led the team in field goal percentage connecting on 53\.3 percent and blocks with 37 on the season\.

She scored a career-high 30 points and pulled down a career-high 22 rebounds against Houston\. She was named to the Women’s College Hoops\.com All-Tournament team and earned third team All-Conference USA honors\.

While at Auburn she was named third team All-SEC by the Associated Press her junior season\. In her final season at Auburn she averaged 12\.4 points and 6\.4 rebounds per game\.

Nero is now looking forward to life as a professional athlete\. “I’m excited to get to play with some experienced people, people who can help me and teach me along the way,” said Nero\. “I’m nervous and it’s kind of intimidating a little bit\. I know they’re going to be working hard and I’m going to be working hard I hopefully should fit in quite nicely\.”

# From Basement Builds to Battlefield Contracts: How Neros Is Reshaping Pentagon Drone Strategy

Soren Monroe-Anderson and Olaf Hichwa once raced drones as teenagers\. Now their startup stands at the center of the U\.S\. military’s urgent bid to flood the battlefield with cheap, lethal aircraft\. The pair founded Neros in 2023\. Barely two years later the company secured one of the Pentagon’s largest small-drone deals to date\.

An Army indefinite-delivery contract worth up to $500 million will supply the service with Neros’s Archer quadcopters through June 2031\. The agreement flows from the Purpose-Built Attritable Systems program\. It positions the young firm among just three primary manufacturers tapped to push modular first-person-view drones down to the platoon level\. But the story runs deeper than any single deal\. Neros has already shipped tens of thousands of its aircraft to Ukraine\. It maintains an office in Kyiv that supports the country’s war effort against Russian forces\.

The Archer itself measures eight inches across\. It carries a 4\.5-pound payload more than 12 miles\. Crucially it contains zero Chinese components\. That distinction earned Neros a spot on the Pentagon’s Blue UAS approved list\. It also drew sanctions from Beijing\. Such independence sets the drone apart in a market long dominated by low-cost Chinese designs\. And it explains why the Defense Department turned to this startup so quickly\.

Ukraine’s grinding conflict has rewritten the rules of modern ground combat\. Cheap expendable aircraft now define operations in the air just above the trenches\. The U\.S\. military watched closely\. It responded with the Drone Dominance initiative\. That roughly $1\.1 billion effort aims to field some 300,000 low-cost attack drones by the end of 2027\. Yet the Pentagon keeps bumping against hard realities\. Most American-made FPV models still cost multiples of the roughly $5,000 per unit defense officials want to pay\.

Neros offers a different path\. The company has publicly committed to producing one million drones annually by 2028\. It recently moved into Project Millennium\. That 250,000-square-foot facility in Los Angeles dwarfs its previous workspace by a factor of 100\. If the plan succeeds Neros alone could increase total U\.S\. drone manufacturing capacity roughly tenfold\. Current estimates place American output at about 100,000 units per year\.

The Army intends to scale its own purchases dramatically\. Officials talk of lifting annual acquisitions from around 50,000 drones to at least one million within roughly two years\. Such ambitions reflect lessons learned in Ukraine\. There Neros aircraft have provided a reliable alternative to Chinese models\. The firm’s Kyiv presence lets it gather direct feedback from operators under fire\. That loop has sharpened designs faster than traditional defense contractors usually manage\.

Recent developments underscore the momentum\. Breaking Defense reported in June 2026 that Neros leads deliveries under the Pentagon’s Gauntlet 1 competition\. The company has shipped all 2,400 Archer drones ordered so far\. More than 1,000 have been accepted\. Ten other vendors together shipped just 560 units still awaiting final approval\. The gap highlights Neros’s edge in execution\.

Yet production at scale remains a steep challenge\. Cost targets loom large\. The military’s desire for $5,000 drones clashes with the expense of American labor, components and quality controls\. Neros must thread that needle while expanding output by orders of magnitude\. Its founders’ racing background helps\. They understand speed, agility and rapid iteration in ways many aerospace engineers do not\.

The broader Pentagon push gained new structure this summer\. In July 2026 the department created the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems\. This office will oversee tens of billions of dollars in drone programs across air, sea and ground domains\. It reports directly to the deputy defense secretary\. The move signals how seriously leaders now take unmanned technology\. USNI News first detailed the memo establishing the new organization\.

Neros emerged from a crowded field\. The Pentagon in February 2026 selected 25 firms to compete for low-cost one-way attack drone contracts\. The list included the startup alongside Griffon Aerospace, Kratos, Modalai and others\. Defense News covered the announcement\. Many of those companies still wrestle with supply chains and certification hurdles that Neros appears to have cleared\.

Earlier coverage captured the founders’ rapid rise\. The New York Times noted in November 2025 that the 20-somethings had raised $121 million to build military drones\. The article described how Neros won a coveted Army contract and gained traction inside the defense sector\. That funding round fueled the move into larger facilities and the hiring needed to hit aggressive production goals\.

The original reporting that brought Neros to wider attention remains instructive\. TechRadar detailed the $500 million contract and the Ukraine shipments that preceded it\. Company leaders described their work simply\. They spoke of “building a viable alternative to Chinese drones at home\.” The phrase captures both the commercial opportunity and the strategic imperative\.

Success is far from guaranteed\. Scaling to one million drones a year will test every part of the operation\. Suppliers must deliver\. Regulators must keep pace\. The battlefield itself continues to evolve\. Ukrainian forces already face sophisticated Russian electronic warfare, jamming and counter-drone systems\. Neros must iterate designs in real time while managing explosive growth\.

Still the trajectory impresses\. From 30 basement-built prototypes hand-delivered to Ukraine the company has moved to industrial-scale ambitions backed by the world’s largest defense budget\. Its aircraft have proven themselves in combat\. The Pentagon has placed a sizable bet\. And the two former teenage racers now find themselves steering a venture that could help determine the outcome of future conflicts\.

The stakes extend beyond any one firm\. U\.S\. leaders worry openly about China’s massive drone output\. Adversaries produce millions of cheap systems each year\. American forces risk arriving with too few options and at too high a price\. Initiatives like Drone Dominance and the new unmanned systems office represent attempts to close that gap\. Neros sits squarely inside those efforts\.

Its story also reflects larger changes inside the defense industry\. Traditional primes move slowly\. Startups with fresh ideas and low overhead can deliver faster\. The Pentagon has shown increasing willingness to award sizable contracts to younger companies that demonstrate results in Ukraine or other hot spots\. That shift carries risks but also promise\.

Watch the numbers in coming quarters\. Delivery rates\. Acceptance figures\. Production ramp\. Cost per unit\. Each metric will reveal whether Neros can convert early combat validation into sustained industrial capacity\. The Army’s goal of one million drones annually is audacious\. Meeting it will require more than one startup\. Yet Neros has positioned itself to claim a leading share\.

The founders once chased speed on race courses\. They now chase it on factory floors and battlefields alike\. The transition looks complete\. The question is how far the momentum will carry them and the Pentagon that placed trust in their machines\.

# The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Data, Neolab, AI Infrastructure, Defense And AI Coding Lead

0 Shares

*Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U\.S\.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board\.*

*This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s top 10 announced funding rounds in the U\.S\. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here\.*

Databricks is back raising another $5 billion, after it raised that amount eight months ago\. The largest fundings also went to an AI neolab, data center and electricity storage, defense, coding and biotech\. Let’s take a look\.

1\. **Databricks, $5B, data platform:** Databricks has surpassed a $7 billion revenue run rate, with more than 80% year-over-year growth in Q2\. The San Francisco-based company raised $ 5 billion in a funding round led by Coatue, with participation from Blackstone, MGX, T\. Rowe Price, and new investor Sixth Street Growth, and raised its valuation to $190 billion\. Databricks was valued at $134 billion back in December 2025 when the company announced it had surpassed a $4\.8 billion revenue run rate\. From its Series A funding of $13 million in 2013, the 13-year-old company has raised around $25 billion in funding over all time, per Crunchbase data\.

2\. **River AI, $1\.1B, AI reinforcement learning:** Founded earlier this year, River AI raised $1\.1 billion across its seed and Series A rounds led by AMP PBC and General Catalyst, with strategic investment from Nvidia and AMD Ventures\. Its founder, Igor Babuschkin, has been at the center of AI developments at Google DeepMind, OpenAI and xAI over the past decade\. The Palo Alto, California-based company seeks to build AI that is personalized and trained directly on what a company or person needs to accomplish, giving the end user control\.

3\. **Form Energy, $750M, electric grid:** Form Energy raised a Series G funding round led by T\. Rowe Price\. The Massachusetts-based company builds longer-lasting 100-hour batteries for grid electricity storage\. A host of investors participated, including private equity, venture and angels, and infrastructure and climate-focused investors Blindspot Ventures, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, GE Vernova, Gigascale Capital, NGP Energy Technology Partners, Prelude Ventures and the TPG Rise Climate Fund\.

4\. **Neros Technologies, $250M, defense:** Neros Technologies, a defense drone manufacturer and drone interceptor, raised a $250 million Series C led by American Strategic Technology Fund and Sequoia Capital\. The Los Angeles-based company, founded in 2023, has raised $370 million to date, per Crunchbase data\. The company announced that by 2028 it will be building 1 million drones per year\. It has contracts with the U\.S\. military and half a dozen allied countries across Europe, Asia and the Middle East\.

5\. **CodeRabbit, $143M, AI code review:** CodeRabbit, which has developed an open-source AI code review technology used by 150,000 open-source projects and 17,000 customers, according to the company, is on a roll\. London-based Atomico and Los Angeles’ Smash Capital led its Series C, and the Walnut Creek, California-based company plans to set up a London office based on customer interest across Europe\. As coding becomes increasingly automated, code review is critical to determine which projects meet production standards\.

6\. **Point2 Technology, $136M, datacenter networking:** Point2 Technology, which builds interconnect solutions for AI data centers, raised an extension of its Series B led by Korea-based LB Investment, including a strategic investment from Arm Holdings and participation from existing investor Maverick Silicon\. The San Jose, California-based company raised $136 million in the Series B\.

7\. **Bridge to Life, $110M, organ preservation:** Bridge to Life, a 21-year-old organ preservation company, raised a $100 million Series C funding led by Soleus Capital and Lauxera Capital Partners\. The Illinois-based company is developing an organ viability assessment tool to expand the market and will use the proceeds to extend its VitaSmart technology to U\.S\. transplant centers\.

8\. \(tied\) **Aureka Biotechnologies, $100M, protein therapeutics:** Aureka Biotechnologies, an AI-native drug discovery platform, raised $100 million in Series B funding led by Granite Asia\. # Nero’s Bridge emerges from Tiber River as Rome faces water crisis

The remains of an ancient bridge have emerged in Rome’s Tiber River, near St Peter’s Basilica, as weeks with virtually no rain caused water levels to plunge\.

The bridge — known as Nero’s Bridge, named for the former Roman emperor — once connected Rome’s city centre with the Tiber’s right bank\.

“Nero is the most famous person linked to this area, because precisely in Nero’s circus, where the Vatican is now located, the Apostle Peter was martyred,” said Antonella Bonini, an archaeologist at Rome’s cultural heritage superintendency\.

“However, scholars consider the bridge to be older \(than Nero’s era\) — built by Caligula, Nero’s uncle,” she said, adding that it existed as early as 39 AD\.

The Tiber’s flow has fallen below 80 cubic metres per second, about half the historic average for the month of July, according to Giovanni Giganti, coordinator of the Rome civil protection service’s centre for water management\.

“We are facing a major water crisis\. And it is a crisis that is also due to the fact that this winter we did have quite abundant rainfall, but then the dry periods … were quite long,” Mr Giganti said\.
